title: Standard Library Essentials
summary: A tour of the built-in modules you'll reach for constantly: json, datetime, os, and random.

checkpoints.title: Batteries included
checkpoints.content: Python ships with a huge standard library, no installation needed. `json` converts between Python objects and JSON text (`json.dumps`/`json.loads`), `datetime` handles dates and times, `os` talks to the operating system (paths, environment variables), and `random` generates pseudo-random values.
checkpoints.explanation: Reaching for the standard library before installing a third-party package is usually the right default — it's already there, well-documented, and has no extra dependency to manage.

hints.H0: "Batteries included" is Python's own description of its standard library.
hints.H1: json, datetime, os, and random are four of the most commonly used modules.
hints.H2: None of these need pip install — they ship with Python itself.

checkpoints.title: Predict json.dumps output

options.explanation: json.dumps() serializes a Python dict into a JSON-formatted string, ready to write to a file or send over a network.
dumps means 'dump string' — it converts the dict into a string representation, not the original dict object.

options.text: It raises a TypeError because dicts can't be converted to JSON
options.explanation: Dicts with simple key/value types are exactly what json.dumps is built to handle — no error here.

checkpoints.explanation: json.dumps() turns a Python value into its JSON text representation — the reverse operation, json.loads(), parses JSON text back into a Python value.

hints.H0: The name dumps hints at 'dump to a string'.
hints.H1: It returns text, not the original Python object.
hints.H2: It returns a JSON-formatted string like '{"name": "Ada", "age": 30}'.

checkpoints.title: Pick a random item from a list
checkpoints.content: Given `options = ["rock", "paper", "scissors"]` and the random module already imported, write an expression that picks one random item from the list.
checkpoints.explanation: random.choice() takes any sequence and returns one randomly selected element from it — the standard way to pick one item at random.

hints.H0: The random module has a function specifically for picking one item from a sequence.
hints.H1: It takes the sequence itself as its only argument.

checkpoints.title: Predict datetime.now()'s type
checkpoints.content: After `import datetime`, what kind of value does `datetime.datetime.now()` return?

options.text: A datetime object representing the current date and time
options.explanation: datetime.now() returns a datetime object you can format, compare, or extract fields (year, month, hour, ...) from.
It returns a structured datetime object, not a string — you'd call .strftime() on it to get a formatted string.

options.text: An integer number of seconds since 1970
options.explanation: That's what time.time() returns — datetime.now() returns a richer datetime object, not a raw integer timestamp.

checkpoints.explanation: datetime.now() returns a datetime object, which is a structured representation you can format or do date arithmetic with, not a plain string or number.

hints.H0: The datetime module deals in structured objects, not raw text or numbers.
hints.H1: That object holds year, month, day, hour, minute, and second as accessible fields.
hints.H2: It's a datetime object representing the current date and time.
